red.focus: Recognize when emotional force replaces a legal reason
red.summary: An argument may express genuine suffering without establishing who caused it or what legal rule applies. Learn to respect the person harmed while testing the premises supporting a proposed legal conclusion.
checklist: I can distinguish emotional significance from proof of a legal element
I can identify an irrelevant personal attack
I can construct a respectful evidence-based response

sections.title: An Important Story Still Needs a Rule
sections.body_md: A tenant describes frightening conditions in an apartment. The experience matters deeply, but a legal claim requires identifying the landlord's duty and the facts showing a violation. A decision maker should not dismiss the person's suffering merely because it is emotional. Nor should counsel assume that emotional force establishes every element. Separate the harm described, evidence supporting it, governing rule, and available remedy. This makes a powerful story legally usable without exploiting its emotional weight.

sections.title: Attack the Argument, Not the Person
sections.body_md: An advocate dismisses a witness's evidence because the witness has little education. That is an irrelevant attack if education does not affect the witness's opportunity to observe or remember. Relevant credibility questions might involve perception, consistency or personal interest. The difference is why an ad hominem argument can mislead: it substitutes prejudice for examination of the proposition. Careful lawyers protect both truth and dignity by asking what the evidence shows, not whether someone looks respectable.

sections.title: Ask What the Conclusion Requires
sections.body_md: A claimant suffered an injury; therefore the defendant must pay. This conclusion might turn out correct, but injury alone does not establish liability. The argument needs an applicable duty, required causal connection and any other legal conditions. Writing the missing premises exposes what should be investigated. A clear legal argument does not make pain less important. It prevents a genuine injury from being paired with an unsupported accusation or an unavailable remedy.

yellow.focus: Identify statistical and evidentiary fallacies in harm arguments
yellow.summary: Legal disputes can be distorted by treating dramatic examples as typical or overlooking how evidence was selected. Learn to recognize base-rate neglect, survivorship bias and misleading comparisons.
checklist: I can recognize a misleading anecdotal generalization
I can explain why base rates matter
I can identify selection bias in reported injury cases

sections.title: A Dramatic Case Is Not a Frequency
sections.body_md: A news report describes a rare severe accident and concludes that all similar activities are extremely dangerous. The report establishes an event, not its population frequency. To evaluate the risk, ask how many relevant activities occurred, which accidents were recorded and how severity was defined. This does not diminish the individual victim's injury. It prevents the analyst from claiming a general risk unsupported by the available data. Legal policy needs both respect for individuals and reliable aggregate reasoning.
sections.audio_script: A news report describes a rare severe accident and concludes that all similar activities are extremely dangerous. The report establishes an event, not its population frequency. It prevents the analyst from claiming a general risk unsupported by the available data. Legal policy needs both respect for individuals and reliable aggregate reasoning.

sections.title: Base Rates Change Interpretation
sections.body_md: A screening method flags many businesses as likely violators. Even if the test detects most true violations, the proportion of flagged businesses actually violating the law may be low when violations are rare. That is a base-rate problem. A lawyer should examine the underlying frequency, true positive rate and false positive rate rather than announcing that a flag proves guilt. The importance is practical: careless interpretation of risk scores can expose innocent people to serious consequences.

sections.title: The Missing Cases Matter
sections.body_md: A study examines only claimants who won damages and concludes that most injuries lead to successful lawsuits. The sample omits claims that failed, settled or were never filed. This is selection or survivorship bias. To draw a wider conclusion, identify the population the study should represent and how cases entered the dataset. Strong legal reasoning uses evidence for what it can establish and describes the missing observations honestly.

orange.focus: Audit injury arguments for causal and cognitive bias
orange.summary: Advanced advocacy may overstate the effect of a harmful event through confirmation bias or selective evidence. Test competing explanations and distinguish an unjustified inference from a legally supported claim.
checklist: I can distinguish evidence of injury from proof of a defendant's act
I can test the strongest rival explanation

sections.title: Evidence Can Be True and Misleading
sections.body_md: An expert cites three studies associating an exposure with illness but omits ten better-designed studies finding little association. The three studies may be genuine, yet the selection can distort the total evidence. A careful lawyer examines why sources were included or excluded and what each study actually measured. The conclusion should not become stronger simply because the brief contains more vivid quotations. An accurate synthesis weighs the entire relevant body of evidence.

sections.title: Confirmation Bias Shapes Investigation
sections.body_md: Once investigators believe a particular company caused an accident, they may notice facts supporting that belief and overlook maintenance failures by another party. A structured alternative-hypothesis check can reduce this risk. List the principal explanations, the facts each predicts and the evidence capable of distinguishing them. This does not demand treating implausible explanations equally. It makes the preferred causal account earn its weight instead of inheriting the investigator's confidence.

sections.title: Client Welfare Requires Proportionate Claims
sections.body_md: Overstating a claim can harm a genuinely injured client by increasing litigation costs, undermining credibility or delaying effective relief. Understatement can also deny lawful protection. A sound argument identifies proved damage, disputed causes, uncertainty and the actual legal requirements. Where specialist evidence is necessary, the lawyer should obtain it through lawful and reliable methods. The objective is not a dramatic story but a defensible route to recognition and repair.

black.focus: Evaluate epistemic injustice in recognizing legal harm
black.summary: At doctoral depth, examine how a legal system's evidence categories can make certain injuries difficult to prove or even describe. Design reforms that improve inclusion without abandoning the right to contest allegations.
checklist: I can distinguish credibility prejudice from a genuine evidentiary weakness
I can analyze how proof structures affect marginalized people
I can defend safeguards protecting both complainants and respondents

sections.title: A Voice Can Be Discounted Unfairly
sections.body_md: A person reporting repeated coercion may be treated as unreliable because of poverty, language or social stigma rather than weaknesses in the account. This is a form of testimonial injustice. A legal system should test observation, consistency and corroboration while guarding against irrelevant prejudice. Yet taking an account seriously is not the same as treating every claim as conclusively proved. Just adjudication combines respectful hearing with evidence standards applied fairly to all parties.

sections.title: Some Harms Lack Familiar Categories
sections.body_md: A series of small discriminatory acts may form a legally relevant pattern even if no one act seems decisive. Traditional claims designed for isolated events might not capture the experience well. A doctoral analyst asks whether existing doctrine already recognizes cumulative effects and, if not, whether reform is justified. The relevant sources, causation rules and proof burdens must remain explicit. A persuasive moral argument should not pretend that an unrecognized claim is already positive law.

sections.title: Design an Answerable Process
sections.body_md: A fair system might provide language assistance, carefully targeted disclosure, reasons for evidentiary decisions and a meaningful opportunity to challenge unreliable assumptions. Each step has costs and must protect confidentiality and opposing parties' rights. A doctoral proposal should specify who decides, what standards govern and how errors can be corrected. It should also evaluate whether affected people can practically use the process. Legal reasoning is at its best when rigorous proof and human dignity reinforce one another.
